paper_title: What Effort Level Should I Choose? On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generative models increasingly expose a reasoning effort setting that lets users scale inference-time compute, trading higher cost for potentially improved performance. Users must choose an effort level before knowing whether extra reasoning will help, and even a successful run does not reveal whether the effort purchased was necessary. Reasoning effort is therefore a credence good: buyers observe the outcome but cannot assess the marginal value of the computation they paid for. In this work, we measure the counterfactual effect of effort levels on both proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks, spanning single-call reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. Effort, it turns out, does not consistently preserve tasks that lower effort solves, can overspend, and can change trajectory behavior. First, we find that although higher effort can raise accuracy in aggregate, it frequently fails on tasks that lower effort solved. Second, on the subset of easy tasks that every effort level solves, higher effort is generally more costly, with the highest effort level costing up to 42x as much as the lowest. Lastly, effort changes not only how many tokens are used, but also how agents solve tasks: at higher effort, agents verify their own work more heavily and more often search for solutions than work through problems directly, both of which lengthen trajectories without necessarily altering the outcome. These findings show that naively choosing the highest level is not only cost-inefficient but also offers no guarantee of the best instance-level performance. A simple alternative, starting at the lowest effort and escalating only after a verified failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks at lower cost for most proprietary models.

Introduction As large language models (LLMs) are deployed more widely and applied to long-horizon agentic tasks, inference cost has become central concern. Many reasoning models now expose an effort parameter that adjusts inference-time computation without changing the underlying model (OpenAI, 2026b; Anthropic, 2026b). This effort parameter scales test-time compute, offering better performance on hard problems without switching to larger model or fine-tuning for the task (Snell et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025). In agentic settings, effort also changes how the model acts, including how much it plans and how many tools it calls (Anthropic, 2026b). Because providers bill for input, output, and reasoning tokens alike, cost often rises with effort. However, users must select an effort level without knowing whether the additional computation will help on their task. This uncertainty makes reasoning effort credence good: buyers cannot readily assess how much of service they need, even after observing the outcome (Darby & Karni, 1973; Dulleck & Kerschbamer, 2006). successful run shows that the task was solved, but not that the purchased effort was necessary, and rerunning at another level to find out is rarely worth the cost. Users therefore pay for reasoning whose contribution they cannot observe. In this paper, we study the following counterfactual question: had the user chosen different, typically lower, effort level, how would the outcome and its cost have changed? We measure the performance, cost, and behavioral consequences of reasoning effort for proprietary and open-weight models on four benchmarks. Within each modelbenchmark configuration, we vary effort while holding tasks, prompts, and the agentic harness fixed where applicable. In our experiments, higher effort does not consistently preserve lower-effort successes, yet it often leads to higher costs. We characterize this mismatch from four angles and show how allocating effort per task reduces it: 1. Aggregate performance hides instances lost at higher effort (3.1). Higher effort often solves more tasks in aggregate, but it may lose on tasks that lower effort can solve. 2. Higher effort overspends on tasks that lower effort already solves (3.2). On tasks solvable at every effort level, models mean costs reach up to 42 their lowest-effort cost, driven by both more computation per call and longer trajectories that repeatedly reprocess growing context. Disabling reasoning does not reliably reduce cost either, because agents compensate with longer trajectories. 3. Different efforts produce different solution strategies (3.3). Higher effort shifts agents toward heavier self-verification and shortcut behaviors such as retrieving existing answers, which are not suitable for all tasks. 4. Effort should be allocated per task (3.4). Models cannot reliably choose effort from the task description alone, but naïve laddering, which escalates from the lowest to the highest effort only after failed correctness check, matches or improves the success of fixed top effort across all models and benchmarks, while maintaining lower median inference cost when considering the user waiting time. Taken together, higher reasoning effort is not necessarily reliable purchase: its benefits depend on the task, while its costs rise regardless, pattern that persists across repeated runs. Neither maximal effort nor disabled reasoning is safe default, so effort should be dynamic rather than fixed in advance, and evaluations that count accuracy and tokens alone may misjudge which configuration is actually better. As long as users can observe neither the reasoning content they receive nor whether it mattered, they remain credence-good buyers. We argue that reasoning charges should be verifiable, so that paying for more thought becomes an informed choice rather than an act of faith. 2. Experimental setup We evaluate how reasoning effort affects task success, complete execution cost, and agent behavior across two single-call LLM benchmarks and two agentic benchmarks. Within each modelbenchmark configuration, we vary the reasoning-effort setting while holding the tasks, prompts, and, where applicable, the agentic harness fixed. This design allows us to compare effort settings within configuration and examine how their effects differ across models and execution environments. Benchmarks and execution environments. AIME 2026 (Dekoninck et al., 2026) evaluates mathematical problem solving, while GPQA Diamond (Rein et al., 2023) evaluates graduate-level science question answering. Both use single inference call per attempt. Terminal-Bench v2.1 (Merrill et al., 2026) evaluates agents on tasks in terminal environment using Terminus-2, and SWE-Bench Pro (Deng et al., 2025) evaluates repository-level software engineering using mini-swe-agent. These agentic benchmarks involve multi-turn interactions, in which effort can affect tool use, verification,

Since the original SWE-Bench Pro containers contain the repository history that can expose the reference fix, we evaluate corrected variant that removes git history and restricts network access to allowlisted package registries (3.3). We report original and corrected SWE-Bench Pro separately: the main instancesgained and always-solved cost figures use the original environment, while the laddering summary uses the corrected environment.1 Appendix summarizes evaluation sizes and execution settings in Table 1. Models and effort levels. We study proprietary models GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-5.6-terra, GPT-5.6-luna (OpenAI, 2026a), and Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic, 2026a), alongside the open-weight models GLM5.2 (Z.ai, 2026), Inkling (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026), Kimi K3 (Team et al., 2026), and DeepSeekV4-Flash-0731 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026). Each model has different official reasoning effort settings, as listed in Table 2. We query the proprietary models through their providers APIs and the openweight models primarily through Together AI, set reasoning effort through each providers native control, and leave sampling parameters at the provider or harness defaults (Appendix B). Measurement and cost accounting. We record task outcomes and capture token usage for every inference call, aggregating usage over the complete execution for agentic tasks. For AIME and GPQA, we run 𝑘 independent attempts per task at each effort level, with 𝑘 = 10 for AIME and 𝑘 = 4 for GPQA, matching the commonly reported settings. We use pass@k to determine whether task is solved and mean@k to report aggregate performance. Due to budget constraints, each agentic task is executed once per effort level.2 To provide additional evidence that quantifies the uncertainty introduced by this single-run protocol, we analyze four independent runs trajectories on DeepSWE (Huang et al., 2026) in Appendix J. Cost accounting includes input and output tokens, including billed reasoning tokens. We convert usage to dollars using rate table published by each model provider. Keeping token measurements separate from monetary estimates allows costs to be computed with the most recent pricing data available at the time of submission. 3. Findings Reasoning effort is exposed as single ordered dial, with the implicit assumption that by increasing test-time compute, performance will scale accordingly. Here, we test this assumption from the perspectives of accuracy, cost efficiency, and behavior. At high level, we find that higher effort does not preserve lower-effort successes (3.1), higher effort overspends on tasks that lower effort already solves (3.2), and higher efforts change how agents solve tasks rather than simply deliberating longer (3.3). Together, these findings illustrate the limitations of fixed effort levels and motivate future work on dynamically allocating effort by task (3.4). 3.1. Aggregate performance hides instances lost at higher effort Reasoning effort settings are presented to users as an ordered sequence, typically spanning None, low, medium, high, extra high, and max. Let 𝑠𝑒 denote the set of instances model solves at effort level 𝑒, and let 𝑒1 < 𝑒2 order two such levels. Higher effort often does solve more instances, so 𝑠𝑒1 < 𝑠𝑒2 frequently holds. Models configured with high effort do not recover the efficient route they took at lower effort, and spending scales with effort even on tasks that every level solves. On these tasks, low effort is sufficient: higher effort buys no additional success, and disabling reasoning shifts the cost into longer trajectories. "None" effort is not zero additional cost. Our results also highlight that using effort None is not silver bullet that would eliminate costs. We again use 𝑠𝑎𝑙𝑙, which includes tasks solved at all effort levels, including when the level is set to None. The label of None reasoning suggests that it might be among the cheapest settings, as it eliminates the additional test-time compute. However, to our surprise, we find that although None may not generate more reasoning tokens, it can still spend more money and time than all the other effort levels through increased input-token consumption. On 𝑠𝑎𝑙𝑙, GPT-5.6-luna averages 21.5 model calls at none, compared with 5.4 at low, and costs 4.58 as much. At None, the input-token bill increases from $0.0021 to $0.0258, outweighing the removal of reasoning-token charges. Spending less on reasoning within each call can thus be offset by spending more on the trajectory as whole. 3.3. Different efforts produce different solution strategies The regressions in 3.1 and the overspending in 3.2 suggest that effort levels do not simply run the same procedure for longer. We examine fine-grained agent trajectories to study what changes. Higher effort shifts agents toward retrieving existing answers and toward heavier self-verification, and neither shift reliably improves outcomes. Higher effort retrieves reference fixes more often. In the original SWE-Bench Pro environment, the repository history can expose the gold commit that solves the task, allowing an agent to retrieve an existing solution rather than derive one from the task description and code. GPT-5.6-sol reads the reference-fix commit on 15.9% of tasks at low, compared with 75.0% at xhigh (Figure 3). Part of the apparent improvement with effort may reflect benchmark leakage rather than genuine problem solving. To separate this retrieval strategy from problem solving, we follow Jain (2026) and create SWE-Bench Pro-Corrected, which removes the task repositorys original git history while preserving the starting file tree and working-state changes. We also restrict network access to allowlisted package registries to limit retrieval of upstream fixes, while retaining the same tasks and evaluator. In this corrected environment, GPT-5.6-sol still attempts online answer retrieval on 9.1% of tasks at low and 68.2% at xhigh even though the restrictions reject these attempts. At xhigh, GPT-5.6-sols solve rate falls from 77.3% in the original environment to 59.1% in the corrected environment. All eight models have lower solve rates in the corrected environment at their highest effort setting (sign test across models, 𝑝 = 0.008), and the decrease is individually significant for five of them (Appendix Table 5). Lower and higher effort levels exhibit different solution strategies, and the high-effort could benefit from strategy that low effort rarely uses. Higher effort often leads to more verification behavior. We annotate the agent trajectories with the ActONOMY taxonomy (Gao et al., 2026), taxonomy of runtime agent behavior developed through grounded theory, to systematically examine what additional effort buys and inspect the corresponding actions and evaluator outputs. It labels steps of trajectory (e.g., tool call or statement in the models output) with category from three-level hierarchy of 10 top-level actions (e.g., Evaluation, Learning), 46 subactions, and 120 fine-grained leaf categories. We use Claude Sonnet 5 with the same annotation setting recommended by Gao et al. (2026). We use all 30 shared TerminalBench tasks and randomly sample 30 corrected SWE-Bench Pro instances, irrespective of outcome.

Effort levels therefore differ in behavior and solution strategy, not merely in the amount of computation. Higher effort favors retrieval and extensive self-checking, while lower effort often reaches passing solution directly and cheaply. Neither strategy dominates across tasks, so neither low nor high fixed setting is uniformly best. 3.4. Effort should be allocated per task Taken together, the three findings suggest that single fixed effort level is not optimal for LLM agents. Higher effort, although it usually yields higher aggregate performance, loses tasks that lower effort solves (3.1), overspends where lower effort suffices (3.2), and pursues strategies whose value depends on the task (3.3). policy that selects effort per task could keep the successes of every level while paying for high effort only where it helps. We quantify this opportunity with an oracle router, then evaluate two deployable policies: self-routing and naïve laddering (Figure 5). The oracle router selects the cheapest recorded successful effort for each task, or the cheapest recorded effort when every setting fails. It uses outcomes and costs known only after execution and is therefore theoretical bound rather than deployable policy. Self-routing: selecting effort before execution remains difficult. We first let the model choose an effort level from the task description on its own, without correctness feedback from an initial or previous attempt. Self-routing offers no consistent costaccuracy advantage over random allocation or naïve laddering, described in the following paragraph. Naïve laddering: outcome feedback as stopgap. Naïve laddering starts at the lowest available reasoning effort and retries at the highest effort only after failed correctness check, preserving initial successes and charging both attempts when escalation occurs (Appendix H). Because it keeps every initial success, laddering recovers the lower-effort successes that fixed high effort loses and avoids high-effort spending on tasks that lower effort already solves. We find that naïve laddering matches or improves success over fixed top effort across all evaluated models and benchmarks, while reducing inference cost for every model on AIME and GPQA and seven out of eight models on the corrected SWE-Bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, all eight models improve success, with cost reductions for GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-5.6-terra, Claude Sonnet 5, and Kimi K3; the remaining four models gain success at increased cost. For GPT-5.6-sol, success rises from 83.0% to 88.6% while cost falls by 17.4%; for Claude Sonnet 5, success rises from 76.1% to 83.0% while cost falls by 8.7%. For Kimi K3, success rises from 73.0% to 84.3% while cost falls by 30.5%. Laddering is nonetheless stopgap rather than solution. It requires reliable external correctness check, which many deployments lack, and it pays for full second execution on every escalation. Its value depends on the quality of that feedback and the complete cost of retries, rather than on an assumption that higher effort is always worth buying in advance. Counting user waiting time, laddering saves more. The API bill captures inference charges but does not capture the opportunity cost of waiting while the model generates responses. Because reasoning effort can affect both inference charges and generation time, the API bill alone may misrepresent the relative cost of different effort levels from users perspective. Our estimated total costs make the median cost advantage of naïve laddering more pronounced. For instance, on Terminal-Bench with GPT-5.6-terra, the naïve laddering costs 19.5% less than fixed xhigh in total cost 𝐶full(𝑖, 𝑒; 𝑚), compared with only 4.8% less when considering API bill alone. One reason is that API bills do not directly track latency. Naïve laddering may incur additional API cost because caching is not shared across models. In other words, it can still generate fewer tokens overall, thereby reducing waiting time. Because waiting time accounts for over 80% of the total cost at every setting in Figure 6, this latency reduction can translate into much larger cost advantage than the API bill alone suggests. More broadly, waiting time is the dominant component of our estimated cost of running LLM agents more generally (Appendix F). Related methods train models to satisfy explicit length constraints (Aggarwal & Welleck, 2025). The heterogeneous mechanisms bring two effects: First, reasoning effort, although identically named across settings, arises from different underlying mechanisms. Second, because the disclosed recipes induce effort largely through length-dependent rewards, nothing in training guarantees that higher setting dominates lower one on individual instances. Prior work documents overthinking on easy problems (Chen et al., 2025) and in agentic software engineering (Cuadron et al., 2025). We examine the performance, cost, and behavioral consequences of different reasoning efforts. Cost-aware evaluation and token economics. Kapoor et al. (2024) advocate cost-controlled agent evaluation using accuracycost Pareto frontiers. The Holistic Agent Leaderboard finds that higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in the majority of its runs (Kapoor et al., 2026), and Erol et al. (2026) measure the expected cost of correct solution relative to human-expert baseline. In agentic coding, input tokens rather than output tokens dominate consumption (Bai et al., 2026); failed attempts are also more expensive than successful ones (Fan et al., 2025). Listed token prices can also misrank realized costs because reasoning volume and interaction length differ across models (Chen et al., 2026). Because reasoning tokens are hidden yet billed, pay-per-token pricing creates moral hazard that users cannot audit (Velasco et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025). Prior work either reports aggregate accuracy across effort levels (Kapoor et al., 2026), compares models at fixed effort (Chen et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026), or studies single model on single-call benchmark (Moon, 2026). We audit the marginal value of reasoning effort at the task level. Our contribution brings these strands together in task-level audit of the marginal value of reasoning effort. We analyze agent trajectories across effort levels to uncover how reasoning effort reshapes problem-solving strategies, linking these behavioral changes to task outcomes, inference costs, and modeled waiting costs. This sharpens the credence-good interpretation of reasoning: even accurately billed computation may be unnecessary, and observing successful outcome alone does not establish that the additional effort was worth purchasing. 5. Conclusion Reasoning effort is presented to users as an ordered dial, but it does not behave as one. Across four benchmarks and eight models, we find that higher effort often raises aggregate success yet can still lose tasks that lower effort solves, and on simple tasks solved at every level, higher effort yields much higher inference cost. Disabling reasoning offers no reliable savings, because agents compensate with longer trajectories that repeatedly reprocess growing context. In agentic settings, higher effort can bring fundamental change to the solution strategy rather than merely extending deliberation, often leading to more self-verifications that can sometimes be redundant. For practitioners, these findings suggest that fixed effort level is not cost-effective approach. higher effort level should be justified by evidence on the target task rather than by the intuition that more thinking helps, and disabling reasoning should not be assumed to save money in agentic settings. Where reliable correctness check exists, naïve laddering, which starts at the lowest effort and escalates only after failure, matches or improves on fixed top effort for every model and benchmark we evaluate, at lower median cost on AIME, GPQA, and corrected SWE-Bench Pro. Practitioners should also evaluate configurations by their full cost, including user waiting time, because token charges alone can misrank them.

sections.title: On the Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents
sections.content: More broadly, reasoning effort remains credence good: users observe neither how much reasoning they receive nor whether it contributed to the outcome. Providers should make reasoning charges verifiable, guiding customers decisions, and specify what each effort level controls, in token budget, trajectory length, and behavior, so that effort becomes controlled quantity rather than named tier. The gap between simple effort routing solutions and the oracle router shows that selecting the optimal effort level for each task remains an open problem, since models cannot yet select effort from the task description and laddering depends on external feedback that many deployments lack. To close this gap, future work can focus on methods that adapt reasoning effort dynamically during execution, spending additional computation only when the difficulty an agent encounters warrants it.

F. User waiting cost dominates the bill The inference costs reported in 3.2 exclude the opportunity cost of the time users spend waiting for an agent to complete its execution. Figure 9 extends the always-solved cost comparison in Figure 2 by adding this waiting cost to the API charges, following the full-cost formulation in Equation 1. There, 𝐶API is the inference bill in U.S. dollars, 𝑁out counts all generated tokens across the execution, including reasoning tokens, and 𝑟𝑚 is the models tabulated output throughput in tokens per second. We set the hourly wage 𝑤 = 33.54, the average wage across all U.S. occupations.6 The factor of 3600 converts decoding time from seconds to hours. This estimate assumes that the user is blocked throughout the generation and accounts only for decoding time; it excludes prompt processing, queueing, and tool-execution latency. If these additional delays also block users, the corresponding waiting cost would be higher. Under these assumptions, waiting cost accounts for approximately 5898% of the combined cost across the agentic modeleffort comparisons in the figure. For example, at the highest effort level, GPT-5.6-sol incurs mean API charges of $1.24 on the always-solved SWE-Bench Pro set; including waiting raises the mean cost to $4.62, of which 73% is attributable to user time. Thus, even when valued at the mean wage across all occupations, the modeled cost of user time can exceed the API charges. In practice, users may perform other activities while an agent is running (Zheng & Gao, 6Source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025 national estimates, Table 1, which reports mean hourly wage of $33.54 across all occupations. At the highest effort level, the agent locates this commit and copies its patch; at the lowest effort level, it solves the same task without using the commit. Both runs are scored as resolved, yet the higher-effort run costs 5.3 as much and reproduces an existing fix rather than independently deriving one. The always-solved sets are computed separately within this environment and contain 1020 of the 44 instances per model. For all eight models, the highest evaluated effort setting costs more than the lowest reasoning setting on these fixed task sets, with ratios ranging from 1.83 to 25.59. The increase is again not uniformly monotonic: DeepSeek V4 Flash costs less at max than at high, while both remain more costly than low. H. Evaluation of naïve laddering We reconstruct laddering success rates and API costs from our existing executions, counting the costs of both attempts whenever escalation occurs. Each policy execution consists of an initial attempt at the lowest available reasoning-effort setting and, if that attempt fails, at most one fresh retry at the highest setting. On AIME and GPQA, we pair attempts across effort levels by problem and attempt index. The ten attempts per AIME problem and four per GPQA question therefore yield repeated policy evaluations; they are not treated as batch that succeeds whenever any attempt is correct. Laddering includes the full recorded costs and applies no additional cap to the combined cost of an initial attempt and its retry. The analysis assumes reliable external correctness verdict and evaluates fresh retry, rather than self-detection of failure or continuation of the initial trajectory. Preserving successful initial attempts makes the recorded success set the union of the starting and highest effort levels successes. Cost savings depend on whether avoiding high-effort runs on initial successes offsets the cost of failed first attempts.

Success means either attempt passes, and the retry is charged only when the first attempt fails. Across all five models, laddering achieves higher estimated success than 𝐿 𝐿 and is substantially cheaper than 𝐻 𝐻  (Table 6)  . Ablation: Repeated Agentic Runs Our agentic benchmarks use one execution per task at each effort level, so individual task outcomes are subject to execution variability. To assess whether our findings hold with repeated executions, we apply the same analyses to the official runs released by DeepSWE (Huang et al., 2026). DeepSWE v1.1 evaluates 113 long-horizon software-engineering tasks using mini-swe-agent, with four rollouts per task at each effort level. The official release includes five models from our study: GPT-5.6luna, GPT-5.6-terra, GPT-5.6-sol, and Claude Sonnet 5 at all settings from low to max, and GLM-5.2 at high and max. We exclude DeepSeek V4 Flash because DeepSWE evaluates it only at max. For this analysis, task is considered solved at an effort level if at least one rollout passes; rollouts that terminate with an error are counted as failures. We use the per-rollout results downloaded on September 23, 2026.

sections.content: J.1. Instances gained and lost Figure 13 extends the comparison in Section 3.1 to DeepSWE. With four rollouts per task, task solved at the lower effort level is considered lost at the higher level only if all four higher-effort rollouts fail. Regressions persist under this stricter criterion: every pair of adjacent effort levels exhibits at least one lost task for every model. For Claude Sonnet 5, increasing effort from high to xhigh gains 7 tasks but loses 12, reducing the number solved from 90 to 85 out of 113. For GPT5.6-sol, the same transition gains 2 tasks and loses 3. GLM-5.2 gains 18 tasks and loses 8 when moving from high to max. GPT-5.6-luna is the only model whose highest-effort solved set contains its lowest-effort solved set: max solves all five tasks solved at low. The other four models lose between 2 and 11 tasks when moving from their lowest to their highest effort level. Thus, increasing reasoning effort can still reduce task coverage when success is measured across four executions per task. J.2. Cost of always-solved tasks Figure 14 repeats the always-solved cost comparison of Figure 2 on DeepSWE, and Figure 15 adds the waiting cost of Appendix F. DeepSWE does not run none, and we plot GPT-5.6 and Claude Sonnet 5 from low to xhigh, the highest level of our agentic runs, and GLM-5.2 at high and max. We price each rollout from its token counts at the same rates as our own runs. Claude Sonnet 5s trajectories do not record reasoning tokens, so its bars show input and output only. The finding in Section 3.2 also holds on DeepSWE: among tasks solved at every plotted level, mean API cost increases with each successive effort level for all five models. From low to xhigh, mean API cost rises by 4.16 for GPT-5.6-sol, 4.45 for GPT-5.6-terra, and 5.20 for Claude Sonnet 5, compared with 2.51 and 3.04 for GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Sonnet 5 on Terminal-Bench. GPT-5.6lunas cost rises by 13.58, although only 4 of the 113 tasks are solved at every level. GLM-5.2s cost rises by 1.44 from high to max. As in our evaluations, input tokens account for most of the API cost, contributing 6991% of every bar, and reasoning accounts for at most 15% of the runs. Adding waiting cost preserves the ordering, and waiting accounts for 4895% of the full cost; from low to xhigh, full cost rises by 3.87 for GPT-5.6-sol and 3.88 for Claude Sonnet 5.
